title: NVIDIA AI Infrastructure and Operations
notes: CERT SCOPE → Entry-level ops + infra for AI: concepts, HW/SW stack, networking, storage, orchestration, monitoring, virtualization, reference architectures.
AI vs. ML vs. DL → AI: broad goal of intelligent behavior. ML: learns patterns from data. DL: multi-layer neural nets that learn hierarchies of features.
Training vs. Inference → Training = compute + data heavy, long jobs, distributed; Inference = latency-sensitive, throughput-focused, often smaller footprints.
Why GPUs for DL → Massive parallelism (thousands of CUDA cores), high memory bandwidth, tensor cores for matrix ops.
Recent AI surge drivers → Larger datasets, better algorithms (transformers), powerful GPUs (Volta→Ampere→Hopper), cloud elasticity, open-source frameworks.
GPU vs CPU → CPU: few complex cores, low latency, control-heavy tasks. GPU: many simple cores, high throughput, data-parallel tasks.
DPU (Data Processing Unit) → Offloads/accelerates networking, storage, security (e.g., BlueField); frees CPU, isolates noisy neighbors, enables zero-trust.
Common AI use cases → Healthcare (med imaging), Finance (fraud), Retail (recSys), Manufacturing (vision/QC), Automotive (perception/AV), GenAI (LLMs).

NVIDIA software stack (overview) → CUDA, cuDNN (DL primitives), TensorRT (inference optimize), Triton (inference server), NGC containers, GPU Operator (K8s mgmt), DCGM (GPU monitoring), Base Command (fleet mgmt), NVML (telemetry).
NVIDIA training/inference toolchain → Frameworks (PyTorch/TensorFlow) on CUDA/cuDNN; multi-GPU via NCCL; inference via TensorRT + Triton.
Lifecycle (MLOps) high-level → Data ingest/label → Train → Validate → Package (container) → Deploy → Monitor → Retrain (feedback).
Scaling dimensions → Vertical: more GPUs per node (multi-GPU). Horizontal: more nodes (multi-node). Pipelines for data and model parallelism.
Multi-GPU scaling (single node) → Add GPUs to one host; use NVLink/NVSwitch for fast intra-node communication; typical for data/model parallel within a chassis.
Multi-node scaling → Add more GPU nodes; need high-perf fabric (InfiniBand or RoCE), use NCCL/collectives; requires fast storage + scheduler.
Model parallel vs. Data parallel → Data parallel: replicas process different batches then all-reduce. Model parallel: split layers/tensors across devices for very large models.
NVLink → High-bandwidth, low-latency GPU↔GPU interconnect within a node; faster than PCIe.
NVSwitch → Switch fabric for many GPUs all-to-all at NVLink speeds; backbone of DGX platforms.
PCIe vs. NVLink → PCIe: general bus, slower latency/bandwidth; NVLink: specialized high-speed GPU fabric; affects gradient sync and batch sizes.
InfiniBand (IB) → End-to-end low latency, high throughput, RDMA, adaptive routing, in-network computing (SHARP); ideal for AI training clusters.
Ethernet for AI → Ubiquitous, cost-effective; requires tuning (RDMA over Converged Ethernet/RoCE, congestion control, QoS) to near-IB performance.
Network design focus for AI → Bisection bandwidth, non-blocking/low oversubscription fabrics, low latency, uniform jitter, ECN/RED/PFC tuning (if RoCE).
Storage performance (training) → Priorities: fast sequential/random READ, high aggregate throughput, low metadata overhead, cache hot datasets.
Storage types → Local NVMe (fast, limited capacity), NAS (NFS), parallel filesystems (Lustre, GPFS), object storage (S3) for capacity (stage/cache to fast tier).
Best overall storage for AI workloads → Fast read I/O with caching (e.g., local NVMe cache + networked backing store).
Data caching layers → FS-level caching, NVMe cache on nodes, dataset prefetch (e.g., DALI), Triton model repository cache for inference.
I/O bottlenecks symptom → Low GPU utilization despite idle CPU; slow data loader; fix with caching, parallel dataloaders, larger I/O pipeline depth.
Cooling basics → GPUs produce high heat density; design for sustained TDP; manage inlet temps, airflow direction, and pressure zones.
Air cooling → Cost-effective, simple ops; typically efficient up to ~≤30 kW per rack; above this, air becomes inefficient.
Liquid/water cooling → Efficient heat rejection at high density; higher CapEx/complexity; supports >30–50+ kW/rack with better PUE.
Hot aisle/cold aisle containment → Prevents mixing, improves ΔT, lowers fan power, stabilizes inlet temperatures.
Power delivery → Right-size PSUs/PDUs; consider peak draw, redundancy (N+1), phase balance, UPS impacts, and selective rack densities.
Energy-efficient computing → Higher utilization = better efficiency; schedule jobs to align with power/cooling capacity; monitor PUE/WUE.
Reference architectures (DGX BasePOD/SuperPOD) → Validated compute + networking + storage + software blueprints; faster time-to-value; predictable scaling.
DGX systems (e.g., H100) basics → Dense GPUs, NVSwitch fabric, robust cooling, optimized firmware; integrated with IB spine/leaf for cluster buildouts.
Hybrid strategy → Develop/iterate on-prem for control and cost; burst/scale inference or large experiments to cloud; balance cost, latency, compliance.
Containers (NGC) → Pre-tuned GPU-accelerated containers (frameworks, SDKs) for portability and performance; reduces env drift and setup time.
Kubernetes role → Orchestrates containerized apps/services; scheduling, scaling, rolling updates, service discovery; needs GPU Operator for GPUs.
GPU Operator → Automates NVIDIA driver, CUDA runtime, DCGM, device plugin, MIG config on K8s nodes; reduces manual setup.
SLURM role → HPC batch scheduler; partitions/queues, constraints (GRES/GPU), time limits, job arrays; great for controlled resource scheduling.
When to use K8s vs. SLURM → K8s for microservices/inference/DevOps workflows; SLURM for batch training, HPC-style multi-node MPI/NCCL jobs.
MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) → Partition one physical GPU into multiple isolated GPU instances with dedicated SMs/memory/cache; predictable QoS.
vGPU → Share a physical GPU across multiple VMs; flexible tenancy; near bare-metal for many compute profiles when properly configured.
DCGM → NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager for telemetry (utilization, clocks, temps, power), health checks, policies, diagnostics.
BMC → Out-of-band hardware management controller for server monitoring (power, fans, thermals) independent of OS.
Base Command → Fleet-level management for DGX environments (user/project mgmt, job submission, monitoring, data access, collaboration).
Job scheduling essentials → Fairness, priority, quotas, preemption, backfilling; target high GPU utilization with correct job shapes and runtime limits.
Low GPU utilization common causes → Data loader bottleneck, slow storage, network congestion, CPU contention, small batch size, kernel mix inefficiencies.
Fixing low utilization → Profile I/O, raise dataloader workers, use asynchronous prefetch, pin memory, use mixed precision, tune batch sizes, enable caching.
Security & isolation → Use DPUs for offload and micro-segmentation; use MIG for predictable multi-tenant GPU performance; encrypt data in-flight/at-rest.
Observability → Export DCGM metrics (Prometheus/Grafana), track per-namespace/job GPU hours, alert on temps/power/throttling/error counters (Xid).
Networking offloads → In-network reduction (IB SHARP), RDMA, GDR (GPU Direct RDMA) for direct GPU↔NIC reads to cut CPU involvement and latency.
AI in cloud – cost levers → Right-size GPU types, spot instances for non-critical jobs, data locality (avoid egress), autoscaling, reserved capacity.
Cooling vs. density planning → Map heat per rack by GPU count/TDP; use CFD or vendor tools; consider future growth and hot-spare space.
Airflow hygiene → Keep filters clean, blanking panels installed, cable management to prevent airflow impairment, consistent rack face pressures.
Node design considerations → PCIe lanes for NICs/storage, NVLink topologies, CPU core counts for feeding GPUs, memory bandwidth per GPU.
Data pipelines → Use accelerated data loading (e.g., DALI), TFRecord/WebDataset, shard datasets across workers, deterministic seeds for reproducibility.
Checkpointing → Frequent checkpoints to resilient storage; ensures recoverability for long jobs and supports preemption/fault tolerance.
Fault tolerance (multi-node) → Elastic training frameworks, retry logic, job requeue on node failures, health checks, NCCL timeout tuning.
Inference serving basics → Triton supports multiple backends (TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX); model ensembles; dynamic batching; versioned model repos.
Latency vs. throughput tradeoff → Larger batches improve throughput but increase latency; tune per-SLO; pin CPU/GPU affinity for consistent jitter.
Resource quotas → Prevent noisy tenants; per-namespace GPU pod limits (K8s), SLURM QOS limits; enforce fair-share and budgets.
Data governance → Track datasets, lineage, versions; control PII; ensure compliance and reproducibility.
Cooling exam pattern → Cold air efficient/cost-effective at low densities; becomes inefficient beyond ~30 kW/rack; water-cooled efficient but higher cost.
NGC containers benefit (exam) → Faster, portable development/deployment of GPU-accelerated AI apps; not a scheduler or a simulation platform.
Managed Kubernetes model → PaaS (Platform as a Service).
Thermals (exam) → GPUs have high heat output compared to other components; plan cooling accordingly.
Storage (exam nuance) → For training: best read & re-read performance; overall: fast read I/O + caching. Object storage for capacity, not peak perf.
Financial services anti-fraud (exam) → Early warnings on counterparties, faster retrieval and anomaly detection.
Workload mgmt & monitoring (exam) → Ensure efficient resource allocation, job scheduling, and usage checks (utilization, bottlenecks).
SLURM (exam) → Tool to schedule AI workloads on a subset of resources; partitions/constraints select GPUs/nodes.
Multi-GPU (exam) → Add GPUs to a node; distribute data across GPUs; improves compute without network hops.
NVLink purpose (exam) → High-speed GPU-to-GPU data transfer; significantly faster than PCIe.
NVSwitch purpose (exam) → Scales all-to-all GPU comms at NVLink speeds inside a chassis.
DGX BasePOD (exam) → Provides infrastructure + networking + software to accelerate AI workload deployment (validated reference arch).
Kubernetes purpose (exam) → Managing and automating containerized applications (orchestration).
vGPU benefits (exam) → Share one physical GPU across VMs; near bare-metal performance profiles for compute.
MIG benefits → Deterministic performance isolation; good for multi-tenant inference or small training jobs.
Hybrid approach (exam) → Develop/iterate on-prem; deploy/scale in cloud; balances cost/performance.
Ethernet considerations (exam) → Bandwidth, latency, congestion must be engineered; not “unaffected by latency.”
InfiniBand benefits (exam) → Low latency, high throughput, intelligent offloads; boosts distributed training performance.
Operator runbook basics → Node readiness (drivers/firmware), fabric health, job queue health, DCGM alerts, storage headroom, cooling/power capacity.
SRE/ops KPIs → GPU util %, job wait times, job success/fail rate, MTTR on failed nodes, PUE/WUE, cost/GPU-hour.
Change mgmt → Use canary nodes for driver/firmware upgrades; drain/cordon; validate NCCL/RDMA regression tests before fleet rollout.
Capacity planning → Track demand by GPU class, profile by job type (training vs. inference), plan racks/power/cooling/network leaves ahead.
Security ops → Signed containers (NGC), image scanning, runtime seccomp/AppArmor, network policies, DPU microsegmentation, RBAC, audit trails.
Backup/DR → Snapshot model repos, checkpoint stores, cluster configs; test restores; multi-AZ replication for critical inference.
Documentation → Keep reference-arch topology, IP schema, cabling maps, firmware matrix, and recovery SOPs current.
